## **Capstone Project: Cyclistic Bike-Share Analysis using R**

Case Study: How does a bike-share navigate speedy success?

#### Import the important packages

install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)  #helps wrangle data
library(lubridate)  #helps wrangle date attributes
library(ggplot2)  #helps visualize data


# **PROCESS¶**

*combining the 12 csv files into 1 data frame for data transformation
and cleaning in notebook.*

#==========================
# 1. DATA COLLECTION
#===========================

-   Set your working directory to the folder containing your 12 CSV

-   Read all 12 CSV files and combine them into one datafram

-   All 12 files are in the same folder and have the same columns


#=======
# Step 1: Import the library
#=======


library(tidyverse)

#=======
# Step 2: Import the File Path
#=======

folder_path <- "/users/yourname/desktop/folder/trip-data"


#======
# STEP 3: UPLOAD DATA
#======

# Upload Cyclistic datasets (csv files) here

library(readr)

db01 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202301-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db02 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202302-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db03 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202303-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db04 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202304-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db05 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202305-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db06 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202306-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db07 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202307-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db08 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202308-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db09 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202309-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db10 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202310-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db11 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202311-divvy-tripdata.csv"))
db12 <- read_csv(paste0(folder_path, "/202312-divvy-tripdata.csv"))

#=======
# Step 4: Verify the first file loaded properly
#=======

head(db01)


#===============================================
# 2. DATA WRANGLE AND COMBINE INTO A SINGLE FILE
#===============================================

# Combined 12 csv files into 1 big files

library(dplyr)

# Stack individual data frames into one big data frame

all_trips <- bind_rows(db01,db02,db03,db04,db05,db06,db07,db08,db09,db10,db11,db12)

# Verify the results by Refresh in the Environment pane

# To get the total row count (length)

nrow(all_trips)


::: {.output .display_data}
5719787



#====================================
# 3. DATA TRANSFORM AND DATA CLEANING
#====================================


### A. started_at and ended_at Date Match {#a-started_at-and-ended_at-date-match}

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Keep only rows where the start and end dates are exactly the same

all_trips_clean <- all_trips %>%
  filter(as.Date(started_at, format="%d-%m-%Y") == as.Date(ended_at, format="%d-%m-%Y"))

# Preview the first few rows and total row/column count

all_trips_clean

# See a vertical summary of all columns and data types

glimpse(all_trips_clean)

### B. Calculate ride_length into HH:MM:SS {#b-calculate-ride_length-into-hhmmss}

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(hms)


# Calculate ride_length and format as HH:MM:SS

all_trips_clean <- all_trips_clean %>%
  mutate(
    started_at = as.POSIXct(started_at, format = "%d-%m-%Y %H:%M"),
    ended_at = as.POSIXct(ended_at, format = "%d-%m-%Y %H:%M"),
    ride_length = as_hms(difftime(ended_at, started_at, units = "secs"))
  )

# Preview the calculated ride lengths side-by-side

all_trips_clean %>% 
  select(started_at, ended_at, ride_length) %>% 
  head(10)


### C. Convert ride_length into positive and non-zero value {#c-convert-ride_length-into-positive-and-non-zero-value}

library(tidyverse)

# Filter for ride_length greater than or equal to 60 seconds (1 minute)

all_trips_v2 <- all_trips_clean %>%
  filter(ride_length >= 60)

# Check the results

all_trips_v2 %>% 
  select(started_at, ended_at, ride_length) %>% 
  head(10)


### D. Convert ride_length \[HH:MM:SS\] into minute format {#d-convert-ride_length-hhmmss-into-minute-format}

# Create a new column 'ride_length_min'


all_trips_v2$ride_length_min <- as.numeric(as.difftime(all_trips_v2$ride_length, 
                                                        format = "%H:%M:%S", 
                                                        units = "mins"))


# Divide the existing column by 60 to convert from 660 to 11

all_trips_v2$ride_length_min <- all_trips_v2$ride_length_min / 60


# Check the results

all_trips_v2 %>% 
  select(started_at, ended_at, ride_length, ride_length_min) %>% 
  head(10)

### F. Create a column day of week (for example WEEKDAY(started_at,1) where 1 is Sunday & 7 is Saturday {#f-create-a-column-day-of-week-for-example-weekdaystarted_at1-where-1-is-sunday--7-is-saturday}

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Create the day_of_week column

all_trips_v2 <- all_trips_v2 %>%
  mutate(day_of_week = wday(started_at))


# Create a column day

# library(tidyverse)

all_trips_v2 <- all_trips_v2 %>%
  mutate(day = recode(day_of_week,
                      "1" = "Sunday",
                      "2" = "Monday",
                      "3" = "Tuesday",
                      "4" = "Wednesday",
                      "5" = "Thursday",
                      "6" = "Friday",
                      "7" = "Saturday"))

all_trips_v2 %>%

### G. Create a column with month number and name of the month {#g-create-a-column-with-month-number-and-name-of-the-month}

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

all_trips_v2 <- all_trips_v2 %>%
  mutate(
    # Create month number (1, 2, 3...)
    month_num = month(started_at),
    
    # Create full month name (January, February...)
    month_name = month(started_at, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)
  )

# Check the results

all_trips_v2 %>% 
  select(started_at, month_num, month_name) %>% 
  head(10)

# Monthly Distribution

all_trips_v2 %>% 
  count(month_num, month_name)

# Total Rows
all_trips_v2 %>% 
  count()

#### 1. Calculate the mean median max min {#1-calculate-the-mean-median-max-min}


# a. mean(all_trips_v2$ride_length) #straight average (total ride length / rides)

mean(all_trips_v2$ride_length_min)

#Mean value is 14.72983


# b. median(all_trips_v2$ride_length) #midpoint number in the ascending array of ride lengths

median(all_trips_v2$ride_length_min)
# 10

# Median ride length min is 10 min


# c. max(all_trips_v2$ride_length) #longest ride

max(all_trips_v2$ride_length_min)
# 1373

# Maximum ride length min value 1373 min or 23 hrs 28 min (longest ride)


# d. min(all_trips_v2$ride_length) #shortest ride

min(all_trips_v2$ride_length_min)
# 1

# Minimum ride length min is 1 min

# Check the results

all_trips_v2 %>% 
  summarise(
    Mean_Minutes = mean(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median_Minutes = median(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max_Minutes = max(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min_Minutes = min(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

#### 2. Total Number of rides Casual vs Members {#2-total-number-of-rides-casual-vs-members}

library(tidyverse)

all_trips_v2 %>% 
  group_by(member_casual) %>% 
  summarise(
    total_rides = n(),
    percentage = (n() / nrow(all_trips_v2)) * 100
  )

#### 3. Compare Members and Casual users {#3-compare-members-and-casual-users}

# a. Compare Mean value from member vs casual (minute)

aggregate(all_trips_v2$ride_length_min ~ all_trips_v2$member_casual, FUN = mean)

# Mean casual 19.64
# Mean member 11.98 


# b. Compare Median value from member vs casual (minute)

aggregate(all_trips_v2$ride_length_min ~ all_trips_v2$member_casual, FUN = median)

# Median casual 12
# Median member 9


# c. Compare Max value from member vs casual (minute)

aggregate(all_trips_v2$ride_length_min ~ all_trips_v2$member_casual, FUN = max)

# Max casual 1373
# Max member 1356

# d. Compare Min value from member vs casual (minute)

aggregate(all_trips_v2$ride_length_min ~ all_trips_v2$member_casual, FUN = min)

# Min casual 1
# Min member 1


# Check the results

all_trips_v2 %>% 
  group_by(member_casual) %>% 
  summarise(
    Mean_Minutes   = mean(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median_Minutes = median(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max_Minutes    = max(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min_Minutes    = min(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#### 1. Analyze ridership data by type and day of the week {#1-analyze-ridership-data-by-type-and-day-of-the-week}

# Analyze ridership data by type and weekday

all_trips_v2 %>%
  mutate(weekday = wday(started_at, label = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(member_casual, weekday) %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_rides = n(),
    average_duration = mean(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(member_casual, weekday)

#### b) Bike Types Rides by Month

library(tidyverse)

# Calculate monthly counts by bike type and user type
monthly_bike_summary <- all_trips_v2 %>%
  mutate(month_name = fct_reorder(month_name, month_num)) %>%
  group_by(month_name, rideable_type, member_casual) %>%
  summarise(total_rides = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(month_name, rideable_type, member_casual)

# Print the table
print(monthly_bike_summary)

#### c) Bike Types Rides on Day of the Week

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Complete multi-variable breakdown

bike_time_summary <- all_trips_v2 %>%
  
# 1. Create proper ordered time variables
  mutate(
    weekday = wday(started_at, label = TRUE),
    month_name = fct_reorder(month_name, month_num)
  ) %>%
  
# 2. Group by all four requested metrics
  group_by(rideable_type, member_casual, weekday, month_name) %>%
  

# 3. Calculate total rides
  summarise(
    number_of_rides = n(),
    .groups = "drop" # Keeps your notebook environment clean
  ) %>%
  

# 4. Arrange logically to read the data easily
  arrange(rideable_type, member_casual, month_name, weekday)



# View the final summary table in your notebook
print(bike_time_summary)

## 1. Percentage Share: Total Number of Rides {#1-percentage-share-total-number-of-rides}


# Number of Rides by the users with percentage

library(tidyverse)

# 1. Prepare the data
pie_data <- all_trips_v2 %>% 
  group_by(member_casual) %>% 
  summarise(
    total_rides = n(),
    percentage = (n() / nrow(all_trips_v2)) * 100
  )

# 2. Create the pie chart
ggplot(pie_data, aes(x = "", y = total_rides, fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  theme_void() + # Removes background grid and axes
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(percentage, 1), "%")), 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), 
            size = 5, 
            color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of Total Rides: Members vs. Casual Riders",
    fill = "User Type"
  )


## 2. Day of the Week {#2-day-of-the-week}


#### a) Number of rides by rider type


# Number of rides by the users

all_trips_v2 %>%
  mutate(weekday = wday(started_at, label = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(member_casual, weekday) %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_rides = n(),
    average_duration = mean(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop" # 1. Prevents a 'summarise' grouping message
  ) %>%
  arrange(member_casual, weekday) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = weekday, y = number_of_rides, fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) + # 2. Fixes raw numbers (e.g., 100000 to 100,000)
  labs(
    title = "Total Annual Rides by Weekday",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Number of Rides",
    fill = "User Type"
  )


### Visual Results: Number of Rides

-   **Members Dominate Volume:** The columns for member riders will be
    significantly taller than casual riders on weekdays (Monday through
    Friday).

-   **The Weekday Peak for Members:** Member rides will show a clear
    \"bell curve\" or high plateau during the workweek (Tuesday,
    Wednesday, and Thursday usually being the highest).

-   **The Weekend Shift for Casuals:** Casual ridership builds up
    throughout the week and peaks dramatically on Saturday and Sunday.
    On weekends, casual ride volume often matches or even surpasses
    member ride volume.


#### b) Create a visualization for average duration

# Average ride duration in minute by the users in Categoty

all_trips_v2 %>%
  mutate(weekday = wday(started_at, label = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(member_casual, weekday) %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_rides = n(),
    # 1. Use ride_length_min directly since you already calculated it
    average_duration = mean(ride_length_min, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop" # 2. Keeps notebook logs clean
  ) %>%
  arrange(member_casual, weekday) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = weekday, y = average_duration, fill = member_casual)) + # 3. Drop the '/ 60'
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +

    title = "Average Annual Ride Duration by Weekday",

### Visual Results: Average Duration Casual vs Member

-   **Casual Riders Dominate Duration:** The columns for casual riders

-   **The Weekend Spike for Casuals:** You will see a massive peak on
    Saturday and Sunday for casual riders.

-   **Their average ride durations:** often double on weekends compared
    to weekdays (reaching 25--30+ minutes).

-   **Consistent Members:** The columns for member riders will look very

## 3. Seasonal or Monthly wise Analysis {#3-seasonal-or-monthly-wise-analysis}


#### a) Monthly Time-Series Plot

#  Montly wise Rides

library(tidyverse)

all_trips_v2 %>% 
  count(month_num, month_name) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = month_name, y = n, group = 1)) +
  # Changed 'size = 1' to 'linewidth = 1'
  geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) + 
  geom_point(color = "red", size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Trip Distribution",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Total Trips"
  )


### Visual Results:

-   **The Summer Peak (Inverted U-Shape):** The blue line will form a
    dramatic curve that rises sharply in the spring, peaks at the very
    top during the summer months (July and August), and drops heavily in
    the autumn.

-   **The Winter Trough:** The line will hit its lowest points in
    January and February, where trip volume drops close to the bottom of
    the graph.

-   **X-Axis Formatting Note:** Because the code maps x = month_name but
    uses group = 1, the line connects properly. However, if your months
    appear in alphabetical order (April, August, December\...) instead
    of chronological order (January, February, March\...), the line will
    look messy and zig-zagged.


#### b) Compare number of ride

## 5. Rideable or Bike Types {#5-rideable-or-bike-types}

# Rideable or Bike Trends

ggplot(monthly_bike_summary, aes(x = month_name, y = total_rides, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  # Splits the chart into two panels side-by-side: Casual vs Member
  facet_wrap(~member_casual) + 
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Bike Type Preferences by User Type",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Total Trips",
    fill = "Bike Type"
  )

### Visual Results:

-   **The \"Docked Bike\"**: You will see that Members almost never use
    docked bikes. The docked bike bars only appear prominently in the
    Casual rider panels, especially on summer weekends. This indicates
    that casual users often grab whatever is available at tourist
    hotspots, whereas commuters prefer specific dockless/classic setups.

-   **Electric Bike:** While classic bikes heavily dominate during the
    summer peak, electric bikes maintain a highly consistent proportion
    of rides even during the cooler spring and autumn months. Casual
    riders often switch to electric bikes on chilly days to get to
    destinations faster.

-   **The Weekend Shift Pattern:** In the summer rows, you will watch
    the electric and classic bars grow equally for casual riders as the
    week progresses from Monday to Sunday, while members stay strictly
    uniform.

# **ACT**

*The analysis of 5.6 million clean bike trips proves that annual members
and casual riders operate on two completely distinct user models.*

Annual Members

Casual Members

### **Conclusion**

The analysis of **5.6 million trips** concludes that annual members and
casual riders use Cyclistic bikes for entirely different purposes.
**Annual members (64.13%)** and **Casual riders (35.87%)** This analysis
evaluates a full year of bike-sharing dataset trends, comparing the
behavioral patterns of Annual Members and Casual Riders. The final
results reveal two distinct consumer segments: Members use the service
as a functional, daily utility for workplace commuting, while Casual
Riders use it as a flexible, weather-dependent leisure activity.

### **Key Findings**

1.  **Trip Volume vs. Duration ParadoxMembers account** for the highest
    volume of individual trips, but their rides are consistently short
    (average 10--13 minutes).Casual Riders take fewer individual trips
    overall, but their trip duration is significantly longer (often
    double or triple that of members, averaging 25--30+ minutes).

2.  **Weekly & Hourly Rush PatternsMembers peak** heavily from Monday to
    Friday during traditional commute hours (08:00 AM and 05:00 PM).
    Their weekend volume drops.Casual Riders dominate the weekend
    (Saturday and Sunday), with trip volumes building steadily
    throughout the afternoon, peaking between 02:00 PM and 04:00 PM.

3.  **Extreme Weather SeasonalityCasual ridership** is highly volatile
    and climate-dependent. It peaks dramatically in summer (July and
    August) and drops close to zero during cold winter months (January
    and February).Member ridership is resilient. While it decreases in
    winter, a baseline volume of members continues to use the bikes for
    routine transit year-round.

-   **Trip Durations:** Casual journeys average 19.65 minutes, nearly
    doubling the 11.98-minute average of members.

-   **Peak Rush Hours:** Members spike at 8:00 AM and 5:00 PM weekdays;
    casual traffic builds steadily on weekend afternoons.

-   **Busiest Service Days:** Thursday is the peak day for members,
    whereas Saturday heavily dominates for casual riders.

-   **High Seasonality:** Casual demand is highly climate-dependent,
    surging drastically from June to August and bottoming out in
    January.

-   **Bike Preferences:** Electric bikes are the top choice overall.


### **Recommendations & Suggestions**


-   **Launch a \"Weekend Warrior\" Membership:** Create a seasonal or
    weekend-only annual subscription pass to target leisure users
    directly.

-   **Deploy Value-Based App Notifications:** Send casual riders push
    notifications showing how much they would save by upgrading.

-   **Run Geofenced Summer Campaigns:** Target casual users via digital
    ads near parks and tourist corridors from June to August.

-   **Optimize Saturday Fleet Layouts:** Position classic and electric
    bikes at high-demand recreational stations on Friday nights.

-   **Introduce Gamified Milestone Rewards:** Offer casual riders app
    badges or ride discounts for completing longer summer weekend
    routes.
